faqs.question: How do you host a Halloween murder mystery party?
faqs.answer: Write or pick one case with a victim, six to eight suspects and three rounds of clues. Send each guest a character about two weeks ahead, hand out clues in rounds with 20 minutes of questioning each, then collect written accusations before the reveal.

faqs.question: How many people do you need for a murder mystery party?
faqs.answer: Six is the practical minimum, because fewer suspects make the killer easy to spot. Eight lets every guest play a suspect; at twelve, add four detectives in two pairs who question everyone but cannot be accused.

faqs.question: How long does a Halloween murder mystery party last?
faqs.answer: Plan about three hours for eight guests, from a 7 pm arrival to a 10 pm reveal, and about two and a half hours for six. A kids' version runs well in 60 minutes.

faqs.question: When should I send murder mystery party invitations?
faqs.answer: About 14 days ahead: Saturday 17 October for Saturday 31 October 2026, or Sunday 17 October for Sunday 31 October 2027. Ask for replies a week before, so you can recast anyone who drops out.

faqs.question: What should a murder mystery character card include?
faqs.answer: A name and role, a costume cue, a secret, and one thing the player must admit in round 2. Tell every player that only the murderer may lie, and that everyone else may stay silent but never invent.

faqs.question: How do I make a murder mystery fair?
faqs.answer: Put every clue the solution needs on the table before the accusations, introduce the culprit at the start, and rule out ghosts and unknown poisons. Those come from Ronald Knox's 1929 rules for detective stories.

faqs.question: Can I use a ghost or witch as the killer on Halloween?
faqs.answer: Use them as rumours, not culprits. Ronald Knox's second rule rules out supernatural solutions, and a magic answer leaves guests feeling cheated after two hours of deduction.

faqs.question: Who should play the murderer?
faqs.answer: Give the role to your most confident performer, who will enjoy holding a lie all evening. A 2023 study of murder mystery players separates puzzle-solvers from story-lovers, and the killer suits the second group.

faqs.question: How do I run a murder mystery for kids without a murder?
faqs.answer: Swap the death for a missing object, such as a vanished prize pumpkin, and keep the same clue logic. For ages 7 to 11, use teams of three or four with one adult per team, and end with an apology rather than a punishment.

faqs.question: Can a SubhSandesh page send murder mystery invitations?
faqs.answer: No. SubhSandesh's Halloween pages are one-person greeting pages, so they cannot assign characters or collect replies. One suits the friend who could not come or the co-host you want to thank.

article.contentMarkdown:
# Halloween Murder Mystery Party: Run Your Own Whodunit for 6–12 Guests

A Halloween murder mystery party works when you write the case yourself: one victim, six to eight suspects with secrets, three rounds of clues and a solution every guest could reach. Below is a complete original case, "Murder at the Wychmoor Lantern Night", with character cards, nine clues, a host script and a kids' version.

Halloween falls on Saturday 31 October 2026 and Sunday 31 October 2027, so send characters 14 days ahead. Keep each note short: 48.3% of shared SubhSandesh pages are opened on a phone. Expect late replies too: on Raksha Bandhan 2026, the nearest festival we have measured, 49.4% of SubhSandesh pages were built on the day itself (n = 89, a different festival).

## How a Halloween murder mystery party works, in 6 stages

A 2023 study in the *International Journal of Role-Playing* splits a murder mystery game into [six stages: preparation, reading, evidence search, analysis, voting and ending](https://journals.uu.se/IJRP/article/view/308). This party follows that order across one evening of about three hours.

The host is the game master and plays no suspect. Every guest is a suspect, and one is the murderer.

## The case: Murder at the Wychmoor Lantern Night, 31 October

It is Lantern Night at the Wychmoor Allotment Society. At 9:00 pm the members set off on a 30-minute lantern trail in the dark, while chairman Ambrose Pell, the pumpkin-show judge for 22 years, stays in the seed shed to count the prize envelopes.

At 9:18 he messages the group. At 9:40 his niece finds him dead beside the brass judging bell.

### The 8 suspects and their character cards

Each card holds a role, a costume cue, a secret and one thing the player must admit in round 2. Only the murderer may lie; everyone else may stay silent, but never invent.

- **Odette Vale, treasurer (the murderer).** Costume: tweed and a ledger. Secret: you took 600 from the prize fund for your sister's rent; Ambrose found out tonight and you struck him at about 9:25. Your lie: you walked the whole trail.
- **Juniper Ash, Ambrose's niece and heir.** Costume: gardening gloves and a cloak. Secret: you argued with him at 8:40 about selling the land. Admit: the argument.
- **Rook Hartley, lantern carver.** Costume: a carving apron. Secret: a 2009 conviction for forged cheques, which Ambrose used to keep you carving unpaid. Admit: you delivered candles to the shed at 8:50.
- **Marigold Fenn, rival grower.** Costume: a rosette marked "2nd". Secret: this year's entry was bought, not grown. Admit: three years in second place.
- **Silas Crane, vet and assistant judge.** Costume: a tape measure. Secret: you believe Ambrose fixed last year's result for Juniper. Admit: you planned to resign tonight.
- **Barnaby Quill, village gazette reporter.** Costume: a notebook and press card. Secret: you were writing about the land sale and Ambrose threatened to sue. Admit: you walked the trail beside Juniper.
- **Hester Bramble, beekeeper (8+ guests).** Costume: a veiled hat. Secret: the developer is your brother. Admit: you saw Rook at the shed at 8:50.
- **Tobias Grieve, developer's agent (8+ guests).** Costume: a suit and hard hat. Secret: Ambrose raised his price at 8:45. Admit: you left the shed angry.

## Three rounds of clues, played over about 90 minutes

Hand out each round as printed cards, then allow 20 minutes of questioning. Every clue the solution needs is on the table by round 3.

### Round 1: the timeline (3 clues)

- **Clue 1, the group message:** at 9:18 pm Ambrose wrote, "Results at ten sharp. Nobody touches the shed." He was alive at 9:18.
- **Clue 2, the lantern register:** every lantern was signed out at 9:00 and back between 9:33 and 9:36, except Rook's, returned at 9:20.
- **Clue 3, the clay:** the shed path was raked with wet orange clay at 8:30. Clay is on the shoes of Rook, Odette and Juniper.

### Round 2: the motives (3 clues)

- **Clue 4, the stove:** a half-burnt ledger page shows three prize-fund withdrawals in green ink. The minutes book notes that the treasurer signs in green.
- **Clue 5, the letter:** a developer's offer for the allotment land, with Ambrose's draft reply: "Yes, if the vote passes."
- **Clue 6, the wallet:** a 2009 newspaper cutting about forged cheques, with Rook's photograph.

### Round 3: the alibis (3 clues)

- **Clue 7, the cider stall:** the stallholder served Rook at 9:20, 9:27, 9:33 and 9:39; he never left the counter, five minutes from the shed.
- **Clue 8, lantern 7:** Odette's lantern came back with a white, unburnt wick, on a trail with no other light.
- **Clue 9, the far gate:** the trail marshal saw Juniper and Barnaby together at the far gate at 9:25, fifteen minutes from the shed.

## The solution, and why it plays fair by Knox's 1929 rules

Odette did it. Ambrose was alive at 9:18 (clue 1), and only the three guests with clay on their shoes went down the shed path (clue 3). Juniper was at the far gate at 9:25 (clue 9) and got her clay finding the body at 9:40; Rook was at the cider stall from 9:20 (clue 7) and got his at 8:50.

That leaves Odette, whose lantern was never lit, so she never walked the dark trail (clue 8), and whose green ink is on the burnt ledger (clue 4). Rook's cheque cutting (clue 6) is the red herring.

In 1929 the priest and crime writer Ronald Knox set out [ten rules for a fair detective story](https://www.umsl.edu/~gradyf/film/knoxdecalogue.htm). This case keeps three: the criminal is "someone mentioned in the early part of the story", "all supernatural or preternatural agencies are ruled out", and no clue is withheld from the reader. Halloween tempts hosts to blame a ghost, and Knox's second rule is the reason not to. His fifth rule reflects the racial prejudice of its time and has no place at your party.

## Host script: what to say, from 7:00 to 10:00 pm

The host's lines carry the evening, so keep them short. Shift the times to suit your guests:

- **7:00, arrivals:** "Welcome to Lantern Night. Your envelope holds your secret; read it alone."
- **7:30, introductions:** "One minute each: who you are, and how you knew Ambrose."
- **7:45, round 1:** "Ambrose promised results at ten. One of you made sure he never gave them."
- **8:45, round 2:** "Secrets come out now. Admit what your card tells you to admit."
- **9:15, round 3:** "The alibis. Whoever walked in the dark carried a light."
- **9:40, accusations:** "Write a name, how and why. Fold it. No conferring."
- **9:50, the reveal:** "Odette, it is time to tell them about lantern 7."

If you serve dinner, place the main course between rounds 1 and 2 and dessert after the reveal. Menus and seating are a separate job; plan them first, and keep clue cards off the plates.

## Scaling the case for 6, 8 or 12 guests

| Guests | Suspects in play | Extra roles | Clue cards | Run time |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 6 | 6 (drop Hester and Tobias) | Host reads the stallholder and marshal | 9 | About 2.5 hours |
| 8 | All 8 | None | 9 | About 3 hours |
| 12 | All 8 | 4 detectives in 2 pairs, with a second clue set | 18 (2 sets of 9) | About 3 hours |

At six, Rook still admits his 8:50 delivery in round 2, so nothing is lost with Hester. At twelve, detectives question anyone, cannot be accused, and vote with the suspects.

## Invitations with character assignments

Send each guest their character on Saturday 17 October 2026 or Sunday 17 October 2027, and keep the secret for the door. The same 2023 study sorts murder mystery players into [eight types](https://journals.uu.se/IJRP/article/view/308), from "detectives" who play for the puzzle to "actors" who play for the story and "socialisers" who mostly want company.

Cast with that in mind: give Odette to your best actor, Silas or Juniper to your keenest puzzler, and Hester or Tobias to a guest who would rather chat. Sample invitation lines:

- "Lantern Night, 31 October, 7 pm. You are Rook Hartley, lantern carver. Bring an apron and a clean conscience, if you have one."
- "You are Marigold Fenn, second place three years running. Wear your rosette. Your secret waits at the door."
- "Reply by 24 October so nobody plays two suspects."

## Kids' version: The Case of the Vanished Prize Pumpkin, for ages 7–11

Keep the clues and remove the death. At 4:18 pm the prize pumpkin is in the shed; at 4:40 it is gone, and the culprit, Otto the treasurer's helper, cracked it by accident and hid it rather than own up.

Run it in 60 minutes with teams of three or four and one adult per team. A 2026 [Young Dragons evaluation](https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC13531801) of tabletop role-play in ten London schools, for ages 9 to 16, found no statistically significant change in pupils' survey scores (n = 22). Staff still reported turn-taking and teamwork when groups stayed small and stable, so keep teams fixed and end with an apology, not a punishment.

## Where SubhSandesh fits, and where it doesn't

SubhSandesh's Halloween pages are one-person greeting pages with partner, bestie, family and kids modes. They will not assign characters, collect replies or print clues; a group message does that.

For the friend who could not come, the [interactive Halloween card](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-halloween) takes about 5 minutes, with up to six photos and a pumpkin they carve until your word glows. For a co-host, the [premium Halloween page](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-halloween-premium) adds a voice note of up to 60 seconds, up to 12 photos and a reply box, in about 10 minutes. If your partner insists they solved it first, the [Court of Love page](https://subhsandesh.in/court-of-love) puts them on trial with ten funny questions; 90.9% of started SubhSandesh pages are published and shared.

Writing your own case loses to a boxed kit when the party is under a week away. Printing and testing nine clues takes an evening.

## Sources

- Xiong S., Wen R., Zheng H., "Player Category Research on Murder Mystery Games", *International Journal of Role-Playing*, issue 13, 15 May 2023 (full text read).
- Knox R. A., "Detective Story Decalogue", introduction to *The Best Detective Stories of 1928–29* (1929), as reproduced by the University of Missouri–St. Louis.
- El-Osta A. et al., "Imaginative play for inclusion: evaluating the Young Dragons tabletop role-playing intervention in UK schools", *BMC Public Health*, 20 June 2026 (Europe PMC, full text read).

structuralLimitations: No Halloween usage data in facts.md; the lead-time figure is Raksha Bandhan 2026 (n = 89), disclosed in body as a different festival.

Knox's Decalogue: first published in 1929 (introduction to The Best Detective Stories of 1928–29), verified against Wikipedia's citation of the Faber introduction as reprinted by Haycraft; the umsl.edu host labels its copy as from a 1939 edition. US public domain (published 1929, before the 1930 line); Knox died 1957, so UK copyright runs to the end of 2027 — the post quotes two short phrases only. Rule V is racist; the post says so and does not reproduce it.

Xiong et al. 2023's eight-type player model is a conceptual typology built from Bartle and GNS theory and Chinese jubensha practice, not a measured survey; the post describes it as a sorting, not a finding about prevalence.

Young Dragons (2026) is a pilot with matched n = 22 and no significant survey change; the post states the null result and uses only the qualitative facilitation finding. Its sample is ages 9–16, the kids' variant targets 7–11.

Brief check: the task prompt allowed Knox's Decalogue 'if verified'; the 1929 date is right, but the only full-text copy found is a university page, not a public-domain repository, so it counts as a capped domain (umsl.edu, 1 post).

PLOS ONE, Scientific Reports, MDPI, Frontiers (incl. the Front AI murder-mystery turn-taking paper and the Front Public Health 'script killing' paper) all avoided per caps/bans; the PLOS ONE 'script killing' paper was skipped as PLOS ONE is full.
